question:
A circle of radius \(1\) is tangent to a circle of radius \(2.\) The sides of \(\triangle ABC\) are tangent to the circles as shown, and the sides \(AB\) and \(AC\) are congruent. What is the area of \(\triangle ABC?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2006_AMC_10A_Q16_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The circles are tangent to the same two sides, so right triangles formed by their radii will have the same angle at \(A\). This lets us connect the radii to the distances of the centers from \(A\).

Let \(O\) and \(P\) be the centers of the circles of radii \(1\) and \(2\), respectively. Each center has equal perpendicular distances to \(AB\) and \(AC\), so both centers lie on the internal bisector of \(\angle A\). Let this bisector meet \(BC\) at \(M\). Since \(AB=AC\), \(AM\) is also an altitude and \(M\) is the midpoint of \(BC\).

Let \(U\) and \(T\) be the tangency points of the smaller and larger circles with \(AC\). A radius to a tangency point is perpendicular to the tangent, so \(\triangle AOU\) and \(\triangle APT\) are right triangles sharing the same angle at \(A\). They are similar, giving
\[
\frac{AP}{AO}=\frac{PT}{OU}=\frac21.
\]
The circles touch externally, so \(OP=1+2=3\). The smaller circle lies between \(A\) and the larger circle, as shown, so \(AP-AO=3\). Together with \(AP=2AO\), this gives \(AO=3\) and \(AP=6\).

The larger circle is tangent to \(BC\), so \(PM=2\). Hence the triangle's height is \(AM=6+2=8\). The Pythagorean theorem in \(\triangle APT\) gives
\[
AT=\sqrt{6^2-2^2}=4\sqrt2.
\]
Now \(\triangle APT\) and \(\triangle ACM\) are right triangles with the same angle at \(A\). Matching their corresponding legs yields
\[
\frac{CM}{AM}=\frac{PT}{AT},
\qquad
CM=8\cdot\frac{2}{4\sqrt2}=2\sqrt2.
\]
Thus \(BC=2CM=4\sqrt2\), and the area is
\[
\frac12\,BC\cdot AM
=\frac12(4\sqrt2)(8)
=16\sqrt2.
\]
The answer is \(16\sqrt2\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
